question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the line integral
${\int }_{C}10 y\,\text{d}s,$
where $C$ is the section of the curve $x=2 y + 3$ from $(5,1)$ to $(9,3).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $x=x(y),$ Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have

$$
x=x(t)=2 t + 3.
$$

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨2 t + 3,\,t⟩,\,1\le t\le 3
$$

Note that the domain $1\le t\le 3$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2 t + 3)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =2\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2)^2+1^2} \\  & =\sqrt{4+1} \\  & =\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=10 y,$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =10 t \\  & =10 t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}10 y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{1}^{3}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\left(10 t\right)\cdot\left(\sqrt{5}\right)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}10 \sqrt{5} t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{3}10 \sqrt{5} t\,\text{d}t & =\left[5 \sqrt{5} t^{2}\right]_{1}^{3} \\  & =10 \sqrt{5}\left(\frac{3^2}{2}-\frac{1^2}{2}\right) \\  & =10 \sqrt{5}\left(\frac{9}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\right) \\  & =40 \sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/generate/scratch/17592186179718/plots/7f66a155994b570a1d47399f.png)

Evaluate the line integral
${\int }_{C}\frac{2 x}{y}\,\text{d}s,$
where $C$ is the section of the curve $x=y^{2}$ from $(1,1)$ to $(6,\sqrt{6}),$ as shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $x=x(y),$ Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have

$$
x=x(t)=t^{2}.
$$

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨t^{2},\,t⟩,\,1\le t\le \sqrt{6}
$$

Note that the domain $1\le t\le \sqrt{6}$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t^{2})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =2 t\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2 t)^2+1^2} \\  & =\sqrt{4 t^{2}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{4 t^{2} + 1}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=\frac{2 x}{y},$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{2 \left(t^{2}\right)}{t} \\  & =2 t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{2 x}{y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{6}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{6}}\left(2 t\right)\cdot\left(\sqrt{4 t^{2} + 1}\right)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{6}}2 t \sqrt{4 t^{2} + 1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve this using the substitution $u=4 t^{2} + 1,$ $\text{d}u=8 t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{6}}2 t \sqrt{4 t^{2} + 1}\,\text{d}t & =2{\int }_{5}^{25}\sqrt{u}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{8}\right)\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{5}^{25}\frac{\sqrt{u}}{4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\left[\frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{2}{3}u^{3/2}\right]_{5}^{25} \\  & =\left[\frac{u^{\frac{3}{2}}}{6}\right]_{5}^{25} \\  & =\left(\left(\frac{\left(25\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{6}\right)\right)-\left(\left(\frac{\left(5\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{6}\right)\right) \\  & =\left(\left(\frac{125}{6}\right)\right)-\left(\left(\frac{5 \sqrt{5}}{6}\right)\right) \\  & =\frac{125}{6} - \frac{5 \sqrt{5}}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the line integral
${\int }_{C}3 x y^{6}\,\text{d}s,$
where $C$ is the section of the curve $x=\frac{2}{y}$ from $(2,1)$ to $(1,2),$ as shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $x=x(y),$ Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have

$$
x=x(t)=\frac{2}{t}.
$$

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨\frac{2}{t},\,t⟩,\,1\le t\le 2
$$

Note that the domain $1\le t\le 2$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2}{t})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =- \frac{2}{t^{2}}\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(- \frac{2}{t^{2}})^2+1^2} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{4}{t^{4}}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{1 + \frac{4}{t^{4}}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=3 x y^{6},$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =3 \left(\frac{2}{t}\right) t^{6} \\  & =6 t^{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}3 x y^{6}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{1}^{2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\left(6 t^{5}\right)\cdot\left(\sqrt{1 + \frac{4}{t^{4}}}\right)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}6 t^{3} \sqrt{t^{4} + 4}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve this using the substitution $u=t^{4} + 4,$ $\text{d}u=4 t^{3}\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}6 t^{3} \sqrt{t^{4} + 4}\,\text{d}t & =6{\int }_{5}^{20}\sqrt{u}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{5}^{20}\frac{3 \sqrt{u}}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\left[\frac{3}{2}\cdot\frac{2}{3}u^{3/2}\right]_{5}^{20} \\  & =\left[u^{\frac{3}{2}}\right]_{5}^{20} \\  & =\left(\left(\left(20\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}\right)\right)-\left(\left(\left(5\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}\right)\right) \\  & =\left(\left(40 \sqrt{5}\right)\right)-\left(\left(5 \sqrt{5}\right)\right) \\  & =35 \sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

${\int }_{C}\frac{8}{- x + y}\,\text{d}s,$
where $C$ is the section of the curve $x=2 y - 5$ from $(-3,1)$ to $(-1,2),$ as shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $x=x(y),$ Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have

$$
x=x(t)=2 t - 5.
$$

$$

$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=\frac{8}{- x + y},$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{8}{- \left(2 t - 5\right) + t} \\  & =- \frac{8}{t - 5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{8}{- x + y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{1}^{2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\left(- \frac{8}{t - 5}\right)\cdot\left(\sqrt{5}\right)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}- \frac{8 \sqrt{5}}{t - 5}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}- \frac{8 \sqrt{5}}{t - 5}\,\text{d}t & =8 \sqrt{5}{\int }_{4}^{3}\frac{1}{u}\cdot(-1)\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{4}^{3}- \frac{8 \sqrt{5}}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\left[-(8 \sqrt{5})\cdot\ln{u}\right]_{4}^{3} \\  & =\left[- 8 \sqrt{5} \ln{\left(u \right)}\right]_{4}^{3} \\  & =\left(\left(- 8 \sqrt{5} \ln{\left(\left(3\right) \right)}\right)\right)-\left(\left(- 8 \sqrt{5} \ln{\left(\left(4\right) \right)}\right)\right) \\  & =\left(\left(- 8 \sqrt{5} \ln{\left(3 \right)}\right)\right)-\left(\left(- 16 \sqrt{5} \ln{\left(2 \right)}\right)\right) \\  & =8 \sqrt{5} \ln{\left(\frac{4}{3} \right)}\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the line integral
${\int }_{C}\frac{4 x}{y}\,\text{d}s,$
where $C$ is the section of the curve $y^2=6x$ from $(\frac{8}{3},4)$ to $(\frac{9}{2},3 \sqrt{3}).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve can be expressed in the form $x=x(y),$ as follows:

$$
y^2=6x\,⟹\,x=\frac{y^{2}}{6}.
$$

Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have

$$
x=x(t)=\frac{t^{2}}{6}.
$$

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨\frac{t^{2}}{6},\,t⟩,\,4\le t\le 3 \sqrt{3}
$$

Note that the domain $4\le t\le 3 \sqrt{3}$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{t^{2}}{6})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =\frac{t}{3}\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(\frac{t}{3})^2+1^2} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{t^{2}}{9}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{t^{2}}{9} + 1}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=\frac{4 x}{y},$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{4 \left(\frac{t^{2}}{6}\right)}{t} \\  & =\frac{2 t}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{4 x}{y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{4}^{3 \sqrt{3}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{4}^{3 \sqrt{3}}\left(\frac{2 t}{3}\right)\cdot\left(\sqrt{\frac{t^{2}}{9} + 1}\right)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{4}^{3 \sqrt{3}}\frac{2 t \sqrt{t^{2} + 9}}{9}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve this using the substitution $u=t^{2} + 9,$ $\text{d}u=2 t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{4}^{3 \sqrt{3}}\frac{2 t \sqrt{t^{2} + 9}}{9}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{2}{9}{\int }_{25}^{36}\sqrt{u}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{25}^{36}\frac{\sqrt{u}}{9}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\left[\frac{1}{9}\cdot\frac{2}{3}u^{3/2}\right]_{25}^{36} \\  & =\left[\frac{2 u^{\frac{3}{2}}}{27}\right]_{25}^{36} \\  & =\left(\left(\frac{2 \left(36\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{27}\right)\right)-\left(\left(\frac{2 \left(25\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{27}\right)\right) \\  & =\left(\left(16\right)\right)-\left(\left(\frac{250}{27}\right)\right) \\  & =\frac{182}{27}\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the line integral
${\int }_{C}\frac{x}{y}\,\text{d}s,$
where $C$ is the section of the curve $y^2=4x$ from $(\frac{5}{4},\sqrt{5})$ to $(3,2 \sqrt{3}).$

Notice that the given curve can be expressed in the form $x=x(y),$ as follows:

$$
y^2=4x\,⟹\,x=\frac{y^{2}}{4}.
$$

Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨\frac{t^{2}}{4},\,t⟩,\,\sqrt{5}\le t\le 2 \sqrt{3}

Note that the domain $\sqrt{5}\le t\le 2 \sqrt{3}$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{t^{2}}{4})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =\frac{t}{2}\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(\frac{t}{2})^2+1^2} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{t^{2}}{4}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{t^{2}}{4} + 1}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=\frac{x}{y},$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{\left(\frac{t^{2}}{4}\right)}{t} \\  & =\frac{t}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{x}{y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\sqrt{5}}^{2 \sqrt{3}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\sqrt{5}}^{2 \sqrt{3}}\left(\frac{t}{4}\right)\cdot\left(\sqrt{\frac{t^{2}}{4} + 1}\right)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\sqrt{5}}^{2 \sqrt{3}}\frac{t \sqrt{t^{2} + 4}}{8}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve this using the substitution $u=t^{2} + 4,$ $\text{d}u=2 t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\sqrt{5}}^{2 \sqrt{3}}\frac{t \sqrt{t^{2} + 4}}{8}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{8}{\int }_{9}^{16}\sqrt{u}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{9}^{16}\frac{\sqrt{u}}{16}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\left[\frac{1}{16}\cdot\frac{2}{3}u^{3/2}\right]_{9}^{16} \\  & =\left[\frac{u^{\frac{3}{2}}}{24}\right]_{9}^{16} \\  & =\left(\left(\frac{\left(16\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{24}\right)\right)-\left(\left(\frac{\left(9\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{24}\right)\right) \\  & =\left(\left(\frac{8}{3}\right)\right)-\left(\left(\frac{9}{8}\right)\right) \\  & =\frac{37}{24}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the line integral
${\int }_{C}12 x^{6} e^{- 2 y}\,\text{d}s,$
where $C$ is the section of the curve $x=e^{\frac{y}{2}}$ from $(1,0)$ to $(\sqrt{5},\ln{\left(5 \right)}).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $x=x(y),$ Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have

$$
x=x(t)=e^{\frac{t}{2}}.
$$

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨e^{\frac{t}{2}},\,t⟩,\,0\le t\le \ln{\left(5 \right)}
$$

Note that the domain $0\le t\le \ln{\left(5 \right)}$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(e^{\frac{t}{2}})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =\frac{e^{\frac{t}{2}}}{2}\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(\frac{e^{\frac{t}{2}}}{2})^2+1^2} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{e^{t}}{4}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{e^{t}}{4} + 1}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=12 x^{6} e^{- 2 y},$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =12 \left(e^{\frac{t}{2}}\right)^{6} e^{- 2 t} \\  & =12 e^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}12 x^{6} e^{- 2 y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\ln{\left(5 \right)}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\ln{\left(5 \right)}}\left(12 e^{t}\right)\cdot\left(\sqrt{\frac{e^{t}}{4} + 1}\right)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\ln{\left(5 \right)}}6 \sqrt{e^{t} + 4} e^{t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve this using the substitution $u=e^{t} + 4,$ $\text{d}u=e^{t}\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\ln{\left(5 \right)}}6 \sqrt{e^{t} + 4} e^{t}\,\text{d}t & =6{\int }_{5}^{9}\sqrt{u}\cdot\left(1\right)\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{5}^{9}6 \sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\left[6\cdot\frac{2}{3}u^{3/2}\right]_{5}^{9} \\  & =\left[4 u^{\frac{3}{2}}\right]_{5}^{9} \\  & =\left(\left(4 \left(9\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}\right)\right)-\left(\left(4 \left(5\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}\right)\right) \\  & =\left(\left(108\right)\right)-\left(\left(20 \sqrt{5}\right)\right) \\  & =108 - 20 \sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =10 \left(\sqrt{3} \sqrt{t}\right) t \\  & =10 \sqrt{3} t^{\frac{3}{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
